subsection: 5. The design process and garment construction

notes.b: The design process is a set of stages that moves from the brief to a finished, evaluated garment.
points: 1. Define and analyse the brief: identify who the garment is for, its purpose, the occasion, the budget and any constraints.
2. Investigate and research: gather ideas from magazines, fabric samples, pattern books and observation of current trends.
3. Generate possible ideas: sketch several designs, varying line, shape, colour and pattern.
4. Present the ideas: a labelled fashion sketch and a short written description show the chosen design features.
5. Refine the design: adjust the chosen design, the fabric and the trimmings until they meet the brief.
6. Implement: plan the work, select fabric and pattern, cut, construct and finish the garment.
7. Evaluate: assess the finished garment for fit, finish, comfort, function and appearance, and note improvements.
A fashion sketch shows the garment's line, shape, proportion and harmony, and it can show colour and fabric.
The front view and, where needed, the back view show the design features that the sketch must label.
The written description covers colour, design, line, proportion, shape, pockets, seams, neckline, sleeves, fabric and finishes, and accessories.
Each design feature named in the description must be visible in the sketch.
Fabric is chosen for its suitability to the purpose: its absorbency, shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery.
A fabric test sample is washed and dried to check shrinkage before cutting, so the finished garment fits after laundering.
Fabric choice must match the design: a soft drape suits a flowing skirt, while a crisp fabric holds the shape of a tailored jacket.
Notions such as zips, buttons, interfacing, lining and thread should be chosen to match the fabric's care needs and colour.

notes.h: Selecting and reading a commercial pattern
notes.b: A commercial pattern is a full-scale tissue paper pattern sold in a sealed envelope.
points: Choose a simple pattern with few darts and seams for a beginner, and a pattern with an easy-sew range where one is offered.
Skirts and trousers are sized by hip measurement; dresses, shirts, coats and jackets are sized by bust or chest measurement.
Other selection factors include the buyer's preference, the cost of the pattern and the value it offers for the number of garments it can make.
The envelope gives the standard body measurements and the finished measurements of the garment.
The envelope lists the fabric quantity needed for each size and style, and whether the fabric should be plaid or diagonal-matched.
The envelope lists the notions needed, such as buttons, zips, interfacing, lining and trimmings, and the number of pattern pieces.
The envelope shows front and back views and suitable fabrics, and it may include advice on the layout and construction order.
Bust or chest: measure around the fullest part of the bust or the chest.
Waist: measure around the natural waistline, with the tape held comfortably, not pulled tight.
Hips: measure around the widest part of the hips, keeping the tape level all the way round.
Nape to waist: measure from the most prominent bone at the base of the neck down to the waistline.
Inside leg: measure from the crotch down the inside of the leg to the required hemline.

notes.h: Laying out and cutting the pattern
points: Follow the pattern instructions and pin the pattern pieces to the fabric with the fabric folded as directed.
Place the straight grain of the pattern parallel to the selvedge of the fabric, so the garment hangs correctly.
Pattern pieces to be placed on a fold must sit exactly on the fold line, so the garment is symmetrical when opened out.
Take account of the nap, or direction of the pile, and of any pattern or print on the fabric, so that all pieces face the same way.
Keep the fabric flat while pinning and cutting, and cut accurately around the pattern edges.
Diagram: pattern pieces on fabric showing the grain line parallel to the selvedge and a piece placed exactly on the fold.
Stage 1: lay out and cut the pattern pieces.
Stage 2: transfer markings and pin and tack the pieces together to check the fit.
Stage 3: machine sew and assemble the garment, joining seams in the order the pattern gives.
Stage 4: insert fastenings, add trimmings and complete the hems and edges.
Stage 5: press the seams and the finished garment, which removes creases and sets the shape.
Stage 6: evaluate the fit and finish, and note any changes needed.

notes.h: Modifying a commercial pattern (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A commercial pattern is made for a standard figure, so it is often changed to suit a particular person.
points: Lengthen a pattern: cut through the alteration lines, insert tissue paper and redraw the seam and fitting lines.
Shorten a pattern: fold along one of the alteration lines by half the amount to be removed, and redraw the seam and fitting lines.
Alteration lines are marked on the pattern, showing where the length can be changed.
Similar adjustments can change the width of the waist, hip, bust or sleeve by folding along the marked lines.
A pattern is modified when the buyer's measurements differ from the size chosen, or when the design needs a different length or width.
The coursework is worth 100 marks, or 10 per cent of the total marks: a design folder (25 marks) and a garment (75 marks).
The 2027 brief: design and sketch an outfit suitable for a young person to wear on holiday, expressing values, interests and personality; the outfit may be knitted, crocheted or machine stitched.
The candidate sets out the design specifications for the outfit, then makes and evaluates one garment from it.
The garment must include two of three processes: buttons and buttonholes; darts or shaping; a pocket.
The garment must be textile based, show a clear interpretation of the theme, and show progression from Junior Cycle textile skills.
Design folder marks: analysis and research 15, implementation 4, evaluation 6.
Garment marks: design aspects 15, skills and processes 50, finish 10.
The work must be the candidate's own, done under the teacher's supervision, with every source referenced, including any AI-generated material; the completion date is 6 April 2027.

Buttonholes: mark the position and length (the button's diameter plus its thickness) on the right front, at right angles to the edge for a horizontal hole, then work by machine with a buttonhole foot or by hand with buttonhole stitch, and cut the opening last.
Buttons: sew on to match the buttonholes, with a thread shank so the fastened layers lie flat; reinforce on fine or loosely woven fabric.

Darts: transfer the dart markings from the pattern, fold right sides together matching the marks, stitch from the wide end to the point, tie off at the point, and press bust and waist darts towards the centre or down.
Other shaping: gathers, pleats, tucks and princess seams also shape a garment to the body.
Patch pocket: neaten and turn down the top edge as a facing, press under the seam allowances, and topstitch to the garment, reinforcing the top corners.
In-seam pocket: the pocket bag is stitched into a side seam so the opening is hidden.
Each process is interfaced or reinforced where it takes strain, and is pressed as it is made.

keyTerms.definition: The set of requirements a garment must meet, including its purpose, the occasion and the budget.
A drawn design showing the garment's line, shape and features, with labels to explain them.
A full-scale tissue paper pattern for a garment, sold with an envelope that gives sizing and construction information.
The finished, non-fraying edge along each side of a woven fabric.
The line printed on a pattern piece that is placed parallel to the selvedge of the fabric.
The direction of the pile or surface pattern on a fabric, which must be kept the same on all pieces.
A marked line on a commercial pattern along which the pattern can be lengthened or shortened.
Long, temporary hand stitches used to hold pieces together before the garment is machine sewn.

questions.prompt: List the stages that should be followed when laying out and cutting a commercial pattern on fabric.
questions.model: Follow the pattern instructions; fold the fabric as directed. Place the straight grain of the pattern parallel to the selvedge. Place pieces that go on a fold exactly on the fold line. Consider the nap and any print on the fabric so all pieces face the same way. Pin the pieces flat, keep the fabric smooth, and cut accurately around the edges.

questions.prompt: Outline the design process a student would follow to make a garment for a specific brief, and explain how the design is evaluated once it is finished.
questions.model: Define and analyse the brief, identifying the purpose, occasion, budget and constraints of the garment. Investigate and research ideas from magazines, fabric samples and pattern books. Generate several possible ideas and present the best one as a labelled fashion sketch with a written description of its line, shape, colour, pattern, neckline, sleeves, fabric and accessories. Refine the design and select suitable fabric, testing its shrinkage, water repellence and crease recovery, and choose a commercial pattern that matches the wearer's measurements. Implement the design by laying out and cutting the pattern, pinning and tacking to check fit, machine sewing, inserting fastenings and finishing, and pressing. Evaluate the finished garment for fit, finish, comfort, function and appearance, against the original brief, and note any improvements for next time.
